children.description: At 250-280 C the surface of molten Sn-Pb oxidises continuously - tin oxide forms preferentially because it has the lower oxidation potential - so the pot grows a skin of SnO2 with lead oxide and flux in it. The skimmer takes it off, but the formation is unavoidable, which is why wave-solder lines had a person whose whole job was pot maintenance and why the flux was designed to keep the oxide mobile and floatable rather than letting it crust over.

facts.label: Oxide
facts.value: SnO2 with PbO, on the pot surface at 250-280 C

facts.label: Control
facts.value: a cover flux, a rotating skimmer, and frequent skimming

children.note: Standard soldering practice; medium confidence on the quantitative rates.

metal.solder.cleaning.name: Cleaning the flux residue off the board
metal.solder.cleaning.description: A rosin-fluxed board is covered in a sticky, slightly acidic film of flux decomposition products that will corrode the copper and will not accept a conformal coating. In 1982 it was removed in an aqueous machine - a conveyor with spray bars and drying ovens - often followed by a trichloroethane or perchloroethylene vapour degreaser. The cleaning water left the factory through the drain with the lead in it, which is the other half of the 1982 leaded-solder problem and the reason the electronics industry spent the late 1980s arguing about what to do about it.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: aqueous wash with detergents, then trichloroethane or perchloroethylene vapour degrease

facts.label: Water
facts.value: 50-200 litres per board on a heavy-duty line

facts.label: Waste
facts.value: the wash water carried lead and tin; the varnish and resin types were the difficult ones

metal.solder.cleaning.note: The water consumption and the solvent choice are representative; medium confidence.

metal.lead.sintering.name: Roasting/sintering of galena to PbO
metal.lead.sintering.description: The concentrate is roasted in a sinter plant: a travelling grate on which a 1-2 m bed of concentrate is ignited and slowly drawn through with the gas being pulled after the fire. The sulphide oxidises to lead(II) oxide: 2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2. The point of sintering rather than fluidised-bed roasting is that the heat can be high and localised enough to sinter the fine particles into a coherent porous cake, which is exactly what the blast furnace needs to breathe. The sinter is 50-60% Pb and the SO2 - at 10-14% - goes to the acid plant, the same one the copper smelter uses.

facts.label: Sinter machine
facts.value: Dwight-Lloyd travelling grate, ~60-90 m2 of grate area, 1-2 m bed

facts.label: Bed temperature
facts.value: 1100-1250 C in the burn-down zone

facts.label: Sinter
facts.value: 50-60% Pb, 8-15% SiO2, self-fluxing with 15-25% CaO

facts.label: SO2
facts.value: 10-14% to the acid plant

metal.lead.sintering.note: The sinter plant is where lead's energy cost sits; it is a genuinely old process and the dominant sinter machine type in 1982 was the Dwight-Lloyd.

children.name: Dwight-Lloyd sinter strand
children.description: A continuous chain of cast-iron pallets on an endless track about 1.2-1.5 m wide, with the ignition hood at the discharge end. Feed is a mix of concentrate, sinter returns, flux and coke spread to exactly 1-2 m - there is nothing clever about it and it works. The strand advances 1-2 m/min, the fire burns through the bed in about 20 minutes, and the hot sinter is broken off by a set of crusher jaws at the end and tipped into the blast furnace. One machine makes 200-400 t of sinter an hour and runs continuously for years.

facts.label: Grate width
facts.value: 1.2-1.5 m for a single-width strand; multi-width for large smelters

facts.label: Output
facts.value: order 200-400 t of sinter per hour per strand

facts.label: Feed moisture
facts.value: 8-12% - the bed has to hold together

children.name: Self-fluxing sinter mix
children.description: Sinter is not simply roasted concentrate. The mix is designed so the sintered cake is its own flux: the silica that comes with the concentrate is balanced with limestone so the blast furnace slag has a basicity near 1.5-2.0. Anything between about 1.0 and 2.0 works; outside that range the slag either freezes in the furnace or dissolves too much lead. The smelter's metallurgist is balancing silica, iron, calcium and lead every shift.

facts.label: Slag basicity
facts.value: CaO/SiO2 of 1.5-2.0 in the blast furnace

facts.label: Limestone in the mix
facts.value: 15-25% of the mix

children.note: Slag basicity range varies with the ore; medium confidence.

metal.lead.blast-furnace.name: Lead blast furnace reduction to crude lead
metal.lead.blast-furnace.description: A lead blast furnace looks like an iron blast furnace but is only 4-7 m tall, because lead reduces so easily. Self-fluxing sinter, coke and limestone are charged at the top; a blast of 200-350 C air is blown in at the hearth; the PbO is reduced to lead by CO at 1000-1100 C and the metal runs out. The sinter, coke and limestone charge comes down a shaft that is deliberately kept chilled so the metallic lead freezes before it goes further down - if it melted it would run into the tuyeres. Two outputs: crude lead bullion at 950-1050 C at the bottom, and a slag carrying off the iron and silica.

facts.label: Furnace height
facts.value: 4.7-7.5 m (much shorter than an iron furnace)

facts.label: Blast
facts.value: 200-350 C, wet or filtered

facts.label: Reduction
facts.value: PbO + C -> Pb + CO, at 1000-1100 C

facts.label: Chilling
facts.value: the shaft is cooled by sprays so the lead freezes as a sponge above the tuyeres

facts.label: Slag
facts.value: CaO-FeO-SiO2, 15-20% of the sinter charge, sometimes tapped separately

metal.iron.copper-cooler.name: Copper stave hearth cooling
metal.iron.copper-cooler.description: The stave coolers that protect the hearth from 1500 C molten iron are made of copper or copper alloy with a water passage cast into them, because copper conducts heat far better than cast iron. They are a copper industry product, and they are one of the more elegant cross-links in this tree: the blast furnace cannot survive without a copper casting technology. On a modern furnace the stave is cast as a composite with a cast-iron backing and a copper water-cooled front, and about 400-900 staves are fitted.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: copper or copper-iron composite with an internal cooling waterway

facts.label: Count
facts.value: 400-900 staves per furnace

facts.label: Service life
facts.value: years to decades; they fail by fatigue at the waterway

metal.iron.copper-cooler.note: Not established: the 400-900 staves per furnace, the cast-iron-backed composite construction, and failure by fatigue at the waterway. The blast furnace reference confirms water-cooled copper jackets are used in lead blast furnace walls, which is a different vessel from an iron furnace hearth.

metal.steel.ladle.name: Ladle treatment, degassing and the steel's last chemistry
metal.steel.ladle.description: In 1982 the most important development in steelmaking was not the furnace but the ladle. A 1980s steel ladle is a 100-200 t vessel on a rotating turret, and it is where three things happen in sequence. Secondary metallurgy: argon is stirred in to homogenise the temperature and composition and to flush hydrogen and nitrogen. Desulphurisation: calcium or a calcium-bearing reagent is added and stirred, taking the sulphur out as calcium sulphide in a basic slag. Deoxidation and inclusion control: aluminium is added as the last deoxidiser, and in a bottom-pour ladle the whole ladle is streamed through a nozzle to collect the inclusions in the nozzle. This is the technology that made clean, low-inclusion, low-carbon steel a reproducible product, and it is why modern sheet steel for tinplate and for deep drawing exists at all.

facts.label: Ladle
facts.value: 100-200 t on a rotating turret

facts.label: Stirring
facts.value: argon at 0.1-0.5 Nm3/min/t

facts.label: Deoxidation
facts.value: 0.5-2 kg of aluminium per tonne

facts.label: Desulphurisation
facts.value: CaO-Flux or Ca-Si, to below 0.005% S in a few minutes

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: 0.03-0.08% for deep drawing and for tinplate base

metal.steel.ladle.note: Secondary metallurgy was genuinely new in the 1980s. The mechanisms are well established; the exact reagent dosages at any specific plant are not. Medium confidence.

metal.solder.fume.name: Wave-solder flux fume
metal.solder.fume.description: Wave-solder flux fume aerosol of lead oxide and rosin-acid degradation products captured at about 100 mm from the wave.
metal.solder.fume.note: Dust composition representative per the baghouse note.

metal.solder.hood-extraction.name: Hood extraction and baghouse collection
metal.solder.hood-extraction.description: Wave-solder hood local-exhaust ventilation with capture hood and baghouse collecting PbO-rosin dust.

metal.tungsten.trioxide.name: Tungsten trioxide
metal.tungsten.trioxide.description: Tungsten trioxide (WO3) calcine from APT for hydrogen reduction at 500-1000 C to porous tungsten powder with K/Alumina doping.
metal.tungsten.trioxide.note: Not established: APT calcination detail; APT itself has no modelled producer (boundary).
